title: Uncoated structural alloys for very high temperatures in oxidizing environments

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a manufacturable structural alloy system that can carry useful loads for long periods at very high temperatures in oxidizing environments without an applied protective coating. Success would require oxidation resistance and mechanical performance in the same material, including usable components and joints. Surviving heat or forming a protective oxide in an isolated experiment would establish only part of that capability.

A relevant materials challenge is documented in refractory high entropy alloys: the supplied 2024 abstract describes a tradeoff in which alloys with good mechanical properties tend to have poorer oxidation resistance, and vice versa. MET-09 seeks to overcome that tradeoff in a usable structural system. The evidence concerns a particular alloy family and does not establish equivalent limitations across every high-temperature structural alloy.

As a proposed design interpretation, “uncoated” permits a protective oxide scale formed by the alloy itself during exposure. The distinction is between protection supplied by the alloy’s composition and behavior and protection supplied by a separately applied coating. Any claimed demonstration should state its surface preparation and treatments so that this boundary is clear.

significance.text: If achieved, the combination could expand the design space for load-bearing components in hotter oxidizing environments. The supplied study identifies refractory high entropy alloys as candidates for nuclear and other high-temperature applications; overcoming their documented mechanical-property–oxidation tradeoff would make such materials more useful for structural engineering. This is a conditional inference from the materials challenge, rather than an equipment capability demonstrated by the study.

As a system-level possibility, a sufficiently durable uncoated alloy could give designers more freedom in hot-section machinery and other extreme-temperature equipment, including opportunities to reconsider cooling requirements and coating-dependent maintenance. Better engine or plant efficiency would depend on the complete design, operating conditions, component life and successful integration. The supplied evidence establishes no numerical efficiency gain, universal operating-temperature increase or practical temperature ceiling for existing alloys.

The potentially revolutionary feature is the combined structural capability over a useful service life. A higher temperature result alone would not establish that impact if the material could not be manufactured, joined or used reliably. Conversely, a useful advance below 1,600 °C could still matter substantially: that temperature is a proposed demanding target, not an established boundary separating incremental from revolutionary progress.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is an alloy system that combines long-term oxidation resistance, creep strength, toughness, manufacturability and joining under the same demanding operating conditions. The supplied abstract supports the narrower mechanical-property–oxidation tradeoff in refractory high entropy alloys. It does not establish that every listed engineering property is presently deficient, quantify rapid oxidation across refractory alloys generally, or prove that the complete capability remains unavailable.

The reported aluminum-containing alloys formed less porous oxide microstructures and showed improved oxidation resistance. This identifies a relevant direction for alloy design, but the supplied abstract does not establish that these oxides remain protective during long service, repeated thermal cycling or simultaneous mechanical loading. Nor does it establish that the compositional changes preserve the full set of structural properties required for a component.

As an engineering synthesis, the central barriers are maintaining a protective surface while the underlying alloy resists time-dependent deformation and damage, preserving that balance through thermal cycles, and reproducing it in manufactured geometries and joints. Candidate systems would need evaluation for scale integrity, oxidation-related material loss, creep, fatigue and toughness together. These are concrete questions for demonstrating the proposed capability; the available abstract does not diagnose their failure mechanisms or establish solutions.

current_state.text: Kieran Rivers, Bradley Young, Yuanbo T. Tang and colleagues published “Oxidation behaviour of Ti-V-Cr-Nb-Ta and Al-Ti-V-Cr-Ta refractory high entropy alloys: Effects of Nb and Al substitutions” on 10 October 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.matdes.2024.113370. The supplied record describes four refractory alloys tested in air at 1,000 °C. The authors report that the two aluminum-containing alloys formed less porous oxide microstructures and had improved oxidation resistance.

That result is relevant evidence of improved oxidation behavior within the tested compositions and conditions. It does not demonstrate sustained, uncoated structural service at 1,600 °C, establish the combined performance of components and joints, or support extrapolation from 1,000 °C to substantially hotter operation. The supplied abstract provides no numerical oxidation improvement, service duration or complete mechanical-property dataset from which to judge the proposed integrated capability.

The evidence available through the supplied review consists of the University of Birmingham landing page’s abstract and bibliographic information. Although the page links the full article, its contents were not supplied for this assessment. The retained landing-page extraction was reported as untruncated and without extraction issues; the substantive limitation is partial article access. Findings beyond the abstract therefore remain unassessed, rather than disproved.

The supplied materials contain no freshness evidence establishing subsequent progress or confirming that this 2024 study represents the latest state of the field as of 1 November 2026. The record supports a dated experimental advance, while the present availability of the complete MET-09 capability remains unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: independently manufactured, uncoated components and joints sustain application-relevant loads and repeated thermal cycling in representative oxidizing atmospheres for a service-relevant duration. Temperatures approaching or exceeding 1,600 °C would be a demanding target, but neither that temperature nor the testing framework is an established standard supplied by the source. Applications with useful advances at lower temperatures should be assessed against their own requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Uncoated components and joints sustain loaded cycling in oxidizing service conditions

completion_criteria.text: A proposed test program should specify numerical temperatures, stresses, exposure durations, cycling schedules, atmosphere compositions and acceptance limits before testing. It should measure oxidation-related material loss and scale integrity alongside creep, fatigue and toughness, including retained properties after exposure. The aim is to demonstrate that oxidation protection and structural performance coexist under the same service conditions, with manufacturing and joining included in the evaluation.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined service tests demonstrate coexisting oxidation protection and structural performance

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility should include independent production batches and independent testing, with composition, processing, surface preparation, geometry and joint details reported. Integrated component trials should follow material-level tests to establish performance under realistic loading and thermal conditions. These are proposed evidentiary requirements, not criteria prescribed by the cited paper.
completion_criteria.label: Independent batches and testing reproduce performance with reported manufacturing details

completion_criteria.text: A convincing result should state practical boundaries: demonstrated temperature range, atmosphere, load, lifetime, allowable damage, component geometry and manufacturing constraints. Finite experiments can establish breadth within those conditions; they cannot establish suitability for every oxidizing environment or every high-temperature application.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated operating limits and practical manufacturing constraints are stated

related_concepts.text: MET-01, “Predictive metallurgy from composition to lifetime,” could support MET-09 by helping select compositions and predict how oxidation and mechanical damage affect service life. The distinction is between a broadly predictive metallurgy capability and a particular alloy system whose performance must be demonstrated experimentally.

MET-11, “Structural alloys with broadly reliable intrinsic corrosion resistance,” overlaps through protection arising from the alloy itself. MET-09 focuses specifically on very high-temperature oxidation combined with load-bearing performance. The broader corrosion concept may involve other environments and degradation mechanisms, so success in either entry would not automatically establish the other.

MET-06, “A practical structural alloy system for sustained fusion-reactor conditions,” shares the need to combine several demanding properties in manufactured components and joints. Its defining application is sustained fusion-reactor service, whereas MET-09 is defined by very high temperatures in oxidizing environments. The cited abstract’s reference to nuclear applications does not establish fusion-specific suitability.

MET-04, “Structural metals that repeatedly heal fatigue damage in service,” addresses recovery from accumulated damage; MET-09 requires adequate fatigue performance but does not require self-healing. MET-07, “Manufacturable, damage-tolerant bulk metallic glasses,” and MET-08, “Practical room-temperature superplastic forming of common alloys,” share concerns about usable mechanical properties and processing, while pursuing different material structures or forming capabilities. Manufacturability in MET-09 does not imply either bulk metallic-glass behavior or room-temperature superplasticity.

unresolved_issues: Whether any alloy system already meets the complete proposed capability, or made substantial progress after the cited 2024 study, is not established by the supplied freshness evidence.
The full article’s exposure durations, numerical oxidation results, detailed compositions and mechanical-property findings were not available in the supplied review.
Long-term oxide protection, creep, fatigue, toughness, manufacturing reproducibility and joint performance under combined service conditions remain unassessed here.
Application-specific loads, durations, atmospheres, cycling schedules and acceptance thresholds must be defined before the proposed completion criteria can be applied.

brief.title: Metals that carry loads in extreme heat without coatings
possible: Engineers could build parts and joints that carry loads for long periods in extreme heat while exposed to oxygen, without applying a protective coating. The metal mixture itself could form an oxide, a surface layer created by reacting with oxygen, to protect the material beneath.
why: Designers of engines, power plants and other hot machinery would have more freedom to choose operating conditions. Durable parts could reduce dependence on coatings and change cooling and maintenance needs.

sources.who: Kieran Rivers, Bradley Young, Yuanbo T. Tang and colleagues
sources.showed: Replacing niobium with aluminum in heat-resistant metal mixtures produced surface oxides with fewer pores and improved resistance to oxygen attack in air at 1,000 °C.
sources.quote: By replacing Nb with Al, the two Al-containing alloys were observed to form a less porous oxide microstructure, showing significant improvement in their oxidation resistance.
sources.cited_for: Changing a metal mixture's composition can improve its resistance to oxygen attack.
sources.not_established: The tests did not establish long service under load in hotter conditions, including manufactured parts and joints.

sources.who: Akhil Bejjipurapu and colleagues at Purdue University
sources.showed: A preprint reports that computer-guided experiments identified metal mixtures that formed protective aluminum oxide layers in hot air.
sources.quote:
Over six cycles, our model-guided investigation identified two quaternary
alloys that exhibit slow, and decreasing, rates of oxidation resulting from the formation of
dense, adherent, externalα-Al 2O3 scales.
sources.cited_for: Protective surface layers can form on candidate mixtures without being applied separately.
sources.not_established: These candidates for use beneath ceramic coatings have not demonstrated prolonged service as uncoated structural parts.

sources.who: Mi Zhao, Kyosuke Yoshimi and Kentaro Yokoyama
sources.showed: A conference abstract reports resistance to oxygen attack and strength under compression in a titanium-enriched, molybdenum-based mixture. It also reports internal cracks.
sources.quote: The alloy displayed relatively good oxidation resistance.
sources.cited_for: A candidate material showed both heat resistance and mechanical strength in separate tests.
sources.not_established: Separate tests do not establish lasting protection and strength together; internal cracking also limits strength and resistance to fracture.

sources.showed: A molybdenum-based mixture reinforced with titanium carbide particles resisted creep, the slow deformation caused by sustained loading, at extreme temperatures in vacuum.
sources.quote: The increasing rupture strains with decreasing stresses (up to 70%) and moderate strain-rate oscillations in the creep curves
sources.cited_for: Candidate materials can resist sustained loads at extreme temperatures when protected from oxygen.
sources.not_established: Vacuum tests do not establish performance in oxygen or through repeated heating and cooling.

sources.who: H. Choe, J. H. Schneibel and R. O. Ritchie
sources.showed: Boron-containing molybdenum mixtures resisted oxygen damage better than comparison materials. Their internal structure strongly affected resistance to fracture and repeated loading.
sources.quote:
the toughness
and cyclic crack-growth resistance actually increased with increasing temperature
sources.cited_for: Composition and processing affect both oxygen resistance and resistance to cracking.
sources.not_established: The results do not establish all required properties together during prolonged, uncoated service in oxygen.

shown: Purdue researchers reported protective surface layers after a day in hot air. Separately, Tohoku University and Ruhr-University Bochum researchers tested sustained loading in vacuum at temperatures reaching 1,600 °C. These results demonstrate different parts of the required capability.
missing: Long tests would need to establish oxygen protection and load-bearing strength together, including resistance to slow deformation and cracking.
The protective surface would need to remain intact through repeated heating and cooling while the material carries loads.
Manufactured components and joints would need to retain these properties across independently produced batches.

milestones.label: Uncoated parts and joints survive loaded heating cycles
milestones.explanation: Independently made parts and joints would have to carry realistic loads through repeated heating and cooling in oxygen for a useful service life. This would establish the capability in working shapes.

milestones.label: Predefined tests demonstrate protection and strength together
milestones.explanation: Tests with predefined conditions and pass limits would have to measure surface protection, material loss, slow deformation and cracking together. This would establish that manufactured and joined material meets the demands simultaneously.

milestones.label: Independent batches and tests reproduce performance
milestones.explanation: Independent batches and tests would have to reproduce performance with composition, processing, surface and joint details reported, followed by component trials. This would establish repeatability under realistic conditions.

milestones.label: Operating and manufacturing limits are established
milestones.explanation: Results would have to define the tested temperatures, gases, loads, lifetimes, allowable damage, shapes and manufacturing constraints. These boundaries would establish where engineers could use the material.

uncertain: The useful temperature advantage over existing alternatives, and any resulting efficiency or maintenance benefit, remain unquantified.
Required loads, test durations, gases and pass limits depend on the intended application.
Approaching 1,600 °C is a demanding proposed target; useful advances at lower temperatures could also qualify.

page.title: Uncoated ultrahigh-temperature structural alloys
page.definition: A manufactured metallic alloy combines oxidation resistance with resistance to creep, deformation under sustained load, and thermal fatigue at metal temperatures of at least 1300°C. Protection comes from an oxide scale formed by the alloy itself rather than an applied coating.

goal.need: GE’s 2004 development paper identifies a 200°C gap between nickel-superalloy airfoil operation near 1150°C and the 1350°C service target for niobium-silicide composites. It places nickel-superalloy melting near 1350°C. Closing this gap requires oxidation protection and load-bearing properties in the same material.

figures.caption: Material temperatures in GE’s 2004 development paper
figures.note: These are material temperatures, not turbine inlet gas temperatures.

statements.body: GE Global Research and Case Western Reserve University
statements.quote: These composites are being developed for structural applications with service temperatures of up to 1350°C.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, ARPA-E ULTIMATE programme
statements.quote: ULTIMATE teams will develop ultrahigh temperature materials for gas turbine use in the aviation and power generation industries.
statements.context: The announcement of 18 November 2020 covers alloys, coatings and manufacturing processes.

completion.title: One manufactured, uncoated alloy meets the creep, fatigue and oxidation benchmarks together.
completion.criterion: Manufacture three turbine blades with dimensions of 3–6 inches and <1% variation in critical dimensions. Material from that production process must meet all of: creep strain <2% after 100 h at 1300°C and 200 MPa; room-temperature tensile ductility >1.5% and fracture toughness >10 MPa√m; ≥1000 thermomechanical cycles at 0.45% strain, R=−1, between 100°C and 1300°C; and cyclic-oxidation loss <25 μm in 100 h at 1315°C. Perform creep and fatigue testing in laboratory air without applied coatings. An oxide grown from the alloy is permitted.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of ARPA-E ULTIMATE and GE material-development benchmarks; neither source sets this combined uncoated test.
completion.basis: Searched ULTIMATE solicitations and programme reviews, NASA oxidation guidance, and GE refractory-composite goals. No external combined completion test for manufactured, uncoated alloys under loading and oxidation was found. The numerical limits are published benchmarks; the oxidation limit was written for niobium-silicide composites. Requiring one production material and concurrent air exposure is the Atlas synthesis.

milestones.title: An uncoated alloy forms a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
milestones.criterion: An alloy develops a continuous, compact, adherent and chemically stable oxide scale without an applied coating. On 17 December 2025, a preprint reported continuous alumina scales and mass gains <1 mg/cm² after 24 h in air at 1000°C for Al30Mo5Ti15Cr50 and Al40Mo5Ti30Cr25 (at.%; two thermogravimetric experiments per selected alloy). This result is not peer reviewed. In four alloys reported on 10 October 2024, substituting Al for Nb reduced oxide porosity at 1000°C in air; the accessible abstract does not state replicate counts.
milestones.set_by: NASA and GE authors, Design for Oxidation Resistance, ASM Handbook, 1997; a published protective-scale criterion, without a numerical lifetime threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: a continuous, compact, slow-growing oxide layer for oxidation and hot corrosion resistance.

milestones.title: An alloy creeps <2% in 100 h at 1300°C and 200 MPa.
milestones.criterion: ULTIMATE’s laboratory benchmarks require creep strain <2% after 100 h at 1300°C and 200 MPa, room-temperature tensile ductility >1.5%, and fracture toughness >10 MPa√m. The creep atmosphere is unspecified. On 11 July 2018, one MoSiBTiC alloy was reported to rupture after 397 h at 1400°C and 137 MPa in vacuum (one test at that condition); rupture endurance does not establish the creep-strain limit. A 2016 conference abstract reports peak compression stress >700 MPa at 1400°C for one Ti-enriched MoSiBTiC composition; replicate counts are unstated.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E, ULTIMATE Annual Review Meeting, 2025, slide 8; the numerical thresholds appear in a table.

milestones.title: An alloy survives ≥1000 fatigue cycles between 100°C and 1300°C at 0.45% strain.
milestones.criterion: Survive ≥1000 thermomechanical fatigue cycles at the programme’s specified 0.45% strain and strain ratio R=−1, between 100°C and 1300°C. In 2003, four Mo-Si-B alloys were studied; a coarse ingot alloy’s fatigue-crack-growth threshold rose from >5 MPa√m at 25°C to approximately 8 MPa√m at 1300°C. Elevated-temperature fatigue testing used argon, 25 Hz and load ratio 0.1. Those crack-growth measurements do not establish this thermomechanical-fatigue endpoint.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E, ULTIMATE Annual Review Meeting, 2025, slide 8; the threshold appears in a table.

milestones.title: Three alloy turbine blades, with dimensions of 3–6 inches, vary by <1% in critical dimensions.
milestones.criterion: Fabricate three generic alloy turbine blades, with dimensions between 3 and 6 inches, using the manufacturing method approved in ULTIMATE Phase 1. Critical dimensional variation among them must be <1%; internal cooling channels are expected. A 2004 GE paper illustrates an investment-cast niobium-silicide prototype airfoil but does not report a three-blade dimensional comparison.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E, ULTIMATE SBIR/STTR solicitation DE-FOA-0002338, section 7.3.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: The critical dimensional variations shall be less than 1% among three samples.

not_found: No located result establishes the combined completion test in one uncoated production alloy.
No external numerical qualification criterion for joints in this uncoated alloy capability was found.
The Birmingham repository’s full-text PDF returned HTTP 403; its abstract was accessible.
ULTIMATE Table II does not identify whether its 0.45% strain is an amplitude or a range.
